caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Greece's debt is the euro area's most extreme: 105.3% of GDP in 2006 (already the high entry), 104.6% in 2007, then the crisis and GDP collapse drove it to 209.9% in 2020, the series peak, with COVID adding the final layer. The recovery has been real: 179.2% in 2022, projected 145.7% in 2025, on strong nominal growth, primary surpluses, and early repayments of bailout loans. GDP went from $269.1bn in 2006 to a projected $280.5bn in 2025 — two decades with essentially no nominal growth. The debt is long-maturity and mostly official-sector, which makes the ratio look worse than the cash-flow burden.
inflation_management: Greece lived both extremes: deflation during the adjustment (-1.4% in 2014, -1.3% in 2020) as internal devaluation cut wages and prices, and 9.3% in 2022, the series high, on the energy shock. It was 1.3% in 2009. Disinflation to 3.0% in 2024 and a projected 2.9% for 2025 has been slower than the euro-area average as tourism-driven services prices stayed firm. Monetary policy is the ECB's; the Greek-specific story is that internal devaluation did the adjusting a floating currency could not.

key_events.event: Revelation of misreported deficit figures triggered the sovereign debt crisis; first EU-IMF bailout (May 2010).
Second bailout with private-sector debt restructuring — the largest sovereign debt haircut in history (2012).
Referendum on bailout terms (July 2015), capital controls, and a third bailout program.
Bailout exit (August 2018) after the deepest peacetime adjustment in modern European history.
COVID-19: debt hit 209.9% of GDP, the series peak, on the GDP collapse.
Regained investment-grade status (2023); rapid debt decline continued, projected at 145.7% in 2025.

outlook_next_decade: Greece's outlook is the euro area's best turnaround story: primary surpluses, falling debt, investment-grade status, and strong tourism and shipping. The debt ratio will keep falling on growth and repayments, though 145.7% projected for 2025 remains very high. Risks are the external ones — a euro-area slowdown or tourism shock — and whether reform momentum survives political cycles. Inflation should converge to target. The decade's honest assessment: repaired, credible, but still leveraged.
